newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Read-Rite says it spurned Applied. [CORRECTED 20:16 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Read-Rite says it spurned Applied. [CORRECTED 20:16 GMT]

text.p: Read-Rite Corp Chairman Cyril Yansouni on Monday said Applied Magnetics Corp's hostile bid for the Read-Rite followed an earlier proposal from Applied to sell itself to what has become its would-be takeover target.

"We have not had serious discussions in nine months, though we had a bit more in-depth talks in the past month. They were the calling party, and the topic of discussion was for us to acquire them," Yansouni told Reuters in an interview soon after he and his fellow directors rejected Applied stock-swap merger proposal.

"We reached the conlusion that it did not make sense. It is a 180-degree difference of any discussion they said took place and a big misinterpretation," he said, referring to Applied's assertion that it had attempted to strike a friendly deal with Read-Rite for almost a year.
Yansouni said the Applied takeover talks "were for information purposes" and declined to say if any terms had been discussed.
Applied is seeking to exchange 0.679 of its shares for each Read-Rite share, a bid first announced last Tuesday.
By early Monday afternoon, Applied shares were up 2-7/8 to 41-3/4 after Read-Rite rejected its bid.
Based on the ratio and Applied's current stock price, the offer values Read-Rite at about $28.35 a share, less than Read-Rite's market price of $30.88 per share in early afternoon trading.
"Wall Street made up their minds (about the bid) and it made our job easier. But our decision was not based on (the offer) price," Read Rite's chairman told Reuters.
"The decision was based on the continued huge potential for our company as we execute our game plan," he said.

Since the bid was announced, Applied stock has fallen about 22 percent, including the partial rebound on Monday. Read-Rite stock has shed 3.5 percent during a period in which the Dow Jones Industrial average slid 2.15 percent and the Nasdaq composite dropped three percent.

"We don't see anything that they bring to us. The board is absolutely convinced," he said, adding Applied's motivation for a merger was to compensate for its lack of investment in the next generation of computer disk-drive technology.
An Applied spokesman (corrects from Read-Rite) was not immediately available to comment on Yansouni's statements.

Yansouni said Read-Rite's "huge potential," as well as Applied's deficiency, was the investment in production of magneto-resistance disk-drive heads, the next-generation technology that he said would supplant the current inductive heads by 1998.

"The disk drive industry is moving to magneto-resistance. We are right now ramping up very aggressively our magneto technology. In the December quarter, 17 percent of our production was of this type and this quarter it will be in excess of 20 percent. Applied has not invested in this technology and that is why we think they want to do this. They have not invested for the future," Yansouni said.
Read-Rite's goal is to have magneto-resistance heads account for "half or more" of total manufactuing output by the end of calendar year 1997, he said.

When asked if Read-Rite expects to adopt a "poison pill" provision or a staggered board of directors to defend against a takeover, Yansouni declined to respond specifically, though said the board "will do everything it needs to do" to remain independent.
